items.title: WebAssembly's wasm2c sandbox escape. An untrusted WebAssembly module breaks out of the generated C sandbox and executes an arbitrary shell command on the host.
items.one_liner: This is a critical sandbox escape in a common Wasm-to-C compiler that allows RCE via memory corruption.
items.summary: A sandbox escape vulnerability in WebAssembly's wasm2c tool allows an untrusted module to execute arbitrary shell commands on a host. The flaw exists in wasm_rt_allocate_funcref_table(), where a failed calloc() allocation for a table is ignored, leaving the table with a NULL data pointer but a full declared size. This allows a guest to force an allocation failure by declaring a massive table, causing bounds checks to pass and table indices to be treated as absolute addresses. The attacker can then leak the libc address via the GOT and call system() to execute commands, verified on Linux arm64 and amd64.
key_facts: Mechanism: calloc() failure leading to NULL pointer dereference as absolute address
items.bottom_line: Untrusted WebAssembly modules compiled with wasm2c can break out of their sandbox and execute arbitrary code on the host system.

claims.text: The vulnerability allows an untrusted Wasm module to execute arbitrary shell commands.
claims.support_span: An untrusted WebAssembly module breaks out of the generated C sandbox and executes an arbitrary shell command on the host.

claims.text: The bug is caused by ignoring the result of calloc().
claims.support_span: wasm_rt_allocate_funcref_table() in wasm2c/wasm-rt-impl-tableops.inc sets table->size from the module's declared element count and then ignores the result of calloc().

claims.text: The exploit leaks the libc address using the GOT.
claims.support_span: table.get atgot_slot/32 reads the embedder's GOT through the broken table andtable.set stores the result into the module's own globals, where wasm code can read it as an integer. That leaks libc'smalloc address

items.one_liner: A long-standing PostgreSQL flaw allows low-privileged users to escalate to superuser and gain full system control.

items.summary: A security researcher describes their initial approach to Android bug bounty hunting, focusing on the transition from static to dynamic analysis. The process involves analyzing the AndroidManifest.xml for exported components, using JADX for decompilation to trace input flows, and utilizing Burp Suite for API interrogation. The author highlights the challenge of SSL pinning and the necessity of Frida for runtime analysis to bypass security checks and understand execution paths. The narrative emphasizes questioning app assumptions and comparing client-side versus server-side enforcement.
items.bottom_line: Effective Android security testing requires moving beyond static analysis to runtime manipulation and comparing the enforcement gap between the UI, client, and server.

claims.text: The researcher uses JADX to trace how external input enters and moves through the app.
claims.support_span: Then JADX entered the chat. And JADX basically said: ‘Good luck bro.’ Classes. Methods. Strings. URLs. Libraries. WebViews. Auth logic. Security checks. Enough code to make my terminal look like it’s going through something. ’ But I’m not trying to read the entire app. That’s a trap. I’m looking for interesting flows. Where does external input enter? Where does it go?

claims.text: SSL pinning prevents traffic from being captured by proxies like Burp Suite.
claims.support_span: With certificate pinning, the app can additionally verify that the server identity matches what it expects.

claims.text: Frida is used for runtime analysis to see function returns and execution paths.
claims.support_span: Static analysis: ‘This function exists.’ Runtime analysis: ‘This function just ran, returned this value, and changed the execution path.’

items.title: International Operation Disrupts Sality P2P Botnet
items.one_liner: Technical details reveal Sality botnet was taken down by manipulating its 40-minute peer verification cycle with sinkhole IPs.
items.summary: Law enforcement agencies across the US, Romania, Hungary, and Bulgaria collaborated with CrowdStrike and Shadowserver to disrupt the Sality P2P botnet via a coordinated sinkholing campaign on August 31. Security researchers identified a flaw in Sality's 40-minute super-peer verification mechanism, allowing them to purge legitimate peers and inject sinkhole addresses directly into infected bot lists. The intervention severed access to over 15,000 actively commanded nodes across an infrastructure that has impacted 11 million IPs over 20 years.
key_facts: Historic reach: >11 million unique IPs (1 million peak concurrent)
Mechanism: Super-peer reputation table manipulation and sinkholing
items.bottom_line: Defenders eliminated Sality's P2P resiliency by injecting sinkhole entries into automated super-peer reputation loops.

claims.text: Every Sality bot verifies known super peers every 40 minutes to maintain network connectivity.
claims.support_span: Every Sality bot maintains a finite list of known super peers, which are publicly reachable infected machines that form the backbone of the P2P network.
